'''Karen E. Daniels''' is an American [[physicist]] who is a professor of physics at [[North Carolina State University]]. Her research considers the deformation and failure of materials. She is a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]], and serves on their Committee on the Status of Women in Physics. She is also a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]].

== Early life and education ==
Daniels completed a bachelor's degree in physics at [[Dartmouth College]] in 1994.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://danielslab.physics.ncsu.edu/people/karen-daniels/|title=Karen Daniels – Daniels Lab|language=en-US|access-date=2019-03-01}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://physics.dartmouth.edu/news/alumni-highlights-karen-daniels-94|title=Alumni highlights: Karen Daniels '94 {{!}} Department of Physics and Astronomy|website=physics.dartmouth.edu|date=22 May 2018 |access-date=2019-03-02}}</ref> She originally planned to study engineering.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Anonymous|date=2018-05-11|title=Q&A: Looking for Failure|journal=Physics|language=en|volume=11|page=47|bibcode=2018PhyOJ..11...47.|doi=10.1103/Physics.11.47}}</ref> After graduating, Daniels spent three years as a physics teacher at [[Saint Ann's School (Brooklyn)|Saint Ann's School]]. Daniels joined [[Cornell University]] as a graduate student, earning a PhD in 2002.<ref name=":0" /> She was a postdoctoral research associate at [[Duke University]], working on [[Jamming (physics)|jamming]] transitions.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://physics.aps.org/authors/karen_daniels|title=Physics - Karen Daniels|website=physics.aps.org|access-date=2019-03-01}}</ref> At [[Duke University]], Daniels developed a technique that can make a container of granules arrange into a solid-state crystal (freeze) or into a fluid (melt) by changing the rate at which they are shaken.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://today.duke.edu/2005/05/grainchange.html|title=Shake and Stir to Make Granular Materials Change Phases|website=today.duke.edu|language=en|access-date=2019-03-02}}</ref>

== Research and career ==
Daniels joined [[North Carolina State University]] as an assistant professor in 2005.<ref name=":0" /> She is interested in how materials compress, stretch and bend when a force is applied.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Daniels|first=Karen|date=2014-11-03|title=Viewpoint: Pushing on a Nonlinear Material|url=https://physics.aps.org/articles/v7/113|journal=Physics|language=en|volume=7|doi=10.1103/Physics.7.113 |doi-access=free}}</ref>  She specializes in granular materials and their [[force chain]]s, and how networks within [[granular material]]s control their bulk properties.  She developed a way to monitor whether granular materials reach a thermodynamic equilibrium, using plastic granules.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2013-02/ncsu-fit021513.php|title=Force is the key to granular state-shifting|website=EurekAlert!|language=en|access-date=2019-03-01}}</ref>

In 2011, Daniels spent a year as an [[Alexander von Humboldt Foundation]] fellow at the [[Max Planck Institute for Dynamics and Self-Organization]] in [[Göttingen]],<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.ds.mpg.de/123831/convection|title=Convection|website=www.ds.mpg.de|access-date=2019-03-02}}</ref>  coordinating a workshop on complex system's: "Particulate Matter: Does Dimensionality Matter."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=1019151|title=NSF Award Search: Award#1019151 - Workshop Support for "Particulate Matter: Does Dimensionality Matter?"; Max Planck Institute for the Physics of Complex Systems; Dresden, Germany|website=www.nsf.gov|access-date=2019-03-02}}</ref> She worked with [[Haverford College]] to study the naturally arising sound waves of [[granular material]]s.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2018/05/180529153058.htm|title=Researchers listen for failure in granular materials|website=ScienceDaily|language=en|access-date=2019-03-01}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Brzinski|first1=Theodore A.|last2=Daniels|first2=Karen E.|date=2018-05-25|title=Sounds of Failure: Passive Acoustic Measurements of Excited Vibrational Modes|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=120|issue=21|article-number=218003|doi=10.1103/physrevlett.120.218003|pmid=29883186|issn=0031-9007|arxiv=1610.09705|bibcode=2018PhRvL.120u8003B|s2cid=47001956 }}</ref> When the materials experience [[shear stress]], the vibrating grains start to stick to the interface. When the stress becomes too much, several grains slip at once, rearranging into new patterns.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://physicsworld.com/a/granular-materials-emit-characteristic-sounds-before-slipping/|title=Granular materials emit characteristic sounds before slipping|date=2018-06-12|website=Physics World|language=en-GB|access-date=2019-03-01}}</ref> The [[Stick-slip phenomenon|stick-slip]] transition is accompanied by low-frequency vibrational modes.<ref name=":1" /> She demonstrated that sound passes through the areas of a material where particles are tightest together.<ref name=":1" /> Her lab team have investigated how space missions could explore asteroids.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://sciences.ncsu.edu/news/a-zero-gravity-laboratory/|title=A Zero-Gravity Laboratory|date=2019-02-13|language=en|access-date=2019-03-01}}{{Dead link|date=March 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> She was supported by [[NASA]] to conduct experiments in [[Zero Gravity|zero gravity]], and took a group of undergraduates to [[Zero Gravity Corporation]].<ref name=":2" /> She has also looked at [[liquid metal]]s, and demonstrated that applying a low voltage to eutectic gallium-indium can cause it to form snowflake-like crystals.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://scienmag.com/voltage-driven-liquid-metal-fractals/|title=Voltage-driven liquid metal fractals|last=Scienmag|date=2017-10-30|website=Scienmag: Latest Science and Health News|language=en-US|access-date=2019-03-02}}</ref>

Daniels is on the editorial board of ''[[Physical Review Letters]]''.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-09-20 |title=PRL Editorial Team |url=https://journals.aps.org/prl/staff |access-date=2023-03-16 |website=Physical Review Letters |language=en}}</ref> She serves on the [[American Physical Society]] Topical Group on Soft Matter committee.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/units/gsoft/governance/committees/index.cfm|title=Committees|website=www.aps.org|language=en|access-date=2019-03-01}}</ref> Daniels has been involved with activities to increase the representation of women in physics since the start of her career.<ref>{{Cite conference|last1=Zastavker|first1=Yevgeniya V.|last2=Williams|first2=Elvira|last3=Whitten|first3=Barbara|author3-link=Barbara Whitten|last4=Valentine|first4=Jami|last5=Rudati|first5=Juana I.|last6=Ong|first6=Maria|last7=Michelman-Ribeiro|first7=Ariel|last8=Martínez-Miranda|first8=Luz J.|last9=Kay|first9=Laura|date=2006-10-17|title=Women in physics in the U.S.: A progress report|url=https://researchers.dellmed.utexas.edu/en/publications/women-in-physics-in-the-us-a-progress-report|conference=WOMEN IN PHYSICS: 2nd IUPAP International Conference on Women in Physics|volume=795|pages=175–178|doi=10.1063/1.2128320|doi-access=free}}{{Dead link|date=March 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> She is part of the [[North Carolina State University]] [[National Science Foundation|NSF]] ADVANCE award "Developing Diverse Departments".<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://advance.wordpress.ncsu.edu/|title=Advance at NC State – 2012|language=en-US|access-date=2019-03-02}}</ref>
